title: Flagrant denial of justice
subtitle: Not a single Russian state body examined any complaint on the merits. Court, prosecutor, General Prosecutor's Office — each responded with a template or a referral. Under international standards, this constitutes an independent ground for refusing extradition.
intro: Since 2025, more than 15 applications have been filed with courts, the Moscow Region Prosecutor's Office, the General Prosecutor's Office of the Russian Federation, and the Internal Security Department. The result: zero substantive responses. This systemic pattern, under ECtHR standards and UN norms, constitutes a self-standing and sufficient ground for refusing extradition — independently of any assessment of the merits of the charges.

un_block.title: UN Standards: Basic Principles on the Role of Lawyers (1990)
un_block.intro: The Eighth United Nations Congress on the Prevention of Crime adopted the 'Basic Principles on the Role of Lawyers' (Havana, 1990). This document is the authoritative UN standard on access to justice and the professional activity of lawyers. Russia, as a UN member state, is bound to observe it.
un_block.url_label: Full text of the UN Basic Principles on the Role of Lawyers (ohchr.org)

principles.text: All persons are entitled to call upon the assistance of a lawyer of their choice to protect and establish their rights and to defend them in all stages of criminal proceedings.
principles.relevance: Lagovsky is denied the ability to file complaints with Russian courts precisely because he is under criminal prosecution — a closed loop that directly violates Principle 1.

principles.text: Lawyers shall be able to perform all of their professional functions without intimidation, hindrance, harassment or improper interference.
principles.relevance: The criminal prosecution of Lagovsky for providing lawful legal services contradicts Principle 16(a): the very initiation of proceedings against a self-employed lawyer for work performed under contract constitutes improper interference.

principles.text: Lawyers shall not be identified with their clients or their clients' causes as a result of discharging their functions.
principles.relevance: The charge effectively attributes the alleged fraud of Lagovsky's client to the lawyer himself, identifying counsel with the client's affairs — a direct violation of Principle 18.

principles.text: Lawyers like other citizens are entitled to freedom of expression, belief, association and assembly. In particular, they shall have the right to take part in public discussion of matters concerning the law, the administration of justice and the promotion and protection of human rights.
principles.relevance: Closure of access to court on the formal ground of fugitive status effectively deprives Lagovsky of any ability to challenge the charges — in court or through supervisory bodies.

echr_block.title: The ECtHR Standard: What Is a 'Flagrant Denial of Justice'?

paras.text: In Othman (Abu Qatada) v. United Kingdom, Application No. 8139/09, 2012, the ECtHR held that an extradition or expulsion case may raise an issue under Article 6 where the person faces a real risk of a 'flagrant denial of justice' in the receiving State — a breach so fundamental that the very essence of the fair-trial guarantee is destroyed.

In Mamatkulov and Askarov v. Turkey [GC], Applications Nos. 46827/99 and 46951/99, 2005, the Grand Chamber reiterated that, in extradition cases, the risk of a flagrant denial of justice in the destination State must be assessed by reference to the facts the requested State knew or ought to have known at the time of surrender. The extraditing State remains responsible for the foreseeable Convention consequences of its decision.

In Golder v. United Kingdom, Application No. 4451/70, 1975, the Court established that access to a court is an inherent aspect of Article 6. A legal system that blocks any practical route to challenge an accusation or the authorities' conduct attacks the core of the fair-trial guarantee itself.

In Kudła v. Poland [GC], Application No. 30210/96, 2000, the Grand Chamber confirmed that Convention rights require practical and effective remedies, not merely formal channels. Repetitive formulaic refusals and circular referrals are therefore relevant when assessing whether the person has been denied any real avenue of redress.

episodes.title: Moscow Region Prosecutor's Office — 8 Identical Responses (A.A. Mitrokhina, 2025)
episodes.what_happened: Deputy head of department A.A. Mitrokhina signed at least 8 responses to complaints about unlawful criminal prosecution. Each response reproduces the same text: the case was properly opened, the investigation is suspended, the arguments about non-involvement were 'examined' by courts when ordering pre-trial detention. No substantive review of any of the arguments was conducted in any response. Some complaints were simply forwarded to the very body whose conduct was being challenged — the MVD Main Investigation Department. The Prosecutor's Office, mandated to exercise independent supervision, effectively became a relay for the investigating authority's position.
episodes.quote: I clarify that the procedural decisions taken in the criminal case have been reviewed by the regional prosecutor's office, as you have previously been notified on multiple occasions.
episodes.why_flagrant: Article 13 ECHR requires a remedy that is practical and effective in law and in fact. Referring to earlier 'checks' while refusing to engage with new submissions, or sending the complaint back to the very body whose conduct is challenged, does not amount to independent review. In an extradition context, such cumulative defects matter because Othman requires the requested State to ask whether the person is being sent into proceedings stripped of their basic guarantees.
violations: Principle 16(a), UN Basic Principles on the Role of Lawyers

episodes.title: General Prosecutor's Office — 5 Applications, Zero Substantive Responses (S.V. Prokopenko, 2025–2026)
episodes.tag: General Prosecutor's Office · Supreme supervisory body
episodes.what_happened: At least 5 applications were filed with the General Prosecutor's Office of the Russian Federation (OGR-87571-26, OGR-95782-26, OGR-93291-26, OGR-116883-26 and OGR-434122-25). The GPO's position in every case: 'no grounds for intervention', the arguments of non-involvement 'are subject to verification through investigation'. Yet the investigation has been suspended since the fugitive warrant was issued, and no investigative steps are being taken. Notably, the response of 17.03.2026 cited the conviction of other persons as confirmation that the prosecution of Lagovsky in absentia is well-founded — a direct violation of the presumption of innocence.
episodes.quote: Thus, there are currently no grounds for the intervention of the General Prosecutor's Office of the Russian Federation.
episodes.why_flagrant: The General Prosecutor's Office is the highest supervisory prosecutorial authority. If even that level refuses to address the substance of the complaints, the remedy system is not merely weak but effectively closed. For extradition purposes, that matters because the requested State must assess foreseeable consequences: whether the person is being returned to a process in which neither prosecutorial oversight nor any practical avenue of challenge is genuinely available.
violations: Art. 6 §1 ECHR (right to a fair trial)

episodes.title: Moscow City Court: Application Refused (16.10.2025)
episodes.what_happened: On 16 October 2025, the Moscow City Court returned the application without consideration. The official pretext: non-compliance with the formal requirements of Art. 7 of Federal Law No. 59-FZ on the procedure for examining citizens' applications. The operative ground, stated explicitly in the letter signed by Deputy President L.Yu. Ishmuratova: the accused is on the wanted list, the applicant cannot be 'identified'. A court — an institution mandated to hear complaints about rights violations — turned the fact of criminal prosecution itself into grounds for denying access to justice: the person cannot challenge the charge precisely because they are subject to it.
episodes.quote: Taking into account the circumstances noted above, and in particular the impossibility of identifying the applicant, who is wanted, the application is to be left without consideration.
episodes.why_flagrant: The right of access to a court cannot be emptied out by procedural formalism tied to the applicant's status as a wanted person. Golder establishes that court access is an inherent element of Article 6. Where the domestic system uses the accusation itself as the reason not to hear the challenge, that points directly to a risk that the proceedings no longer provide the minimum guarantees required by Article 6.
violations: Principle 1, UN Basic Principles on the Role of Lawyers

conclusion_title: Conclusion: Systemic Denial as an Independent Ground to Refuse Extradition
conclusion_paras: The facts set out above are not a collection of isolated procedural errors. They form a stable system: every authority at every level — from the regional prosecutor to the General Prosecutor's Office and the Moscow City Court — operates on the same template of avoidance. More than 15 applications were filed in total; not one was examined on the merits.

Under the ECtHR approach reflected in Othman v. UK (2012), Mamatkulov and Askarov v. Turkey (2005), Golder v. United Kingdom (1975) and Kudła v. Poland (2000), the requested State must look beyond formal paperwork and assess whether the person is being sent into a process that offers any real access to a court and any effective remedy. If those guarantees are absent in practice, extradition engages the responsibility of the extraditing State.

The UN Basic Principles on the Role of Lawyers (1990), adopted by the Eighth UN Congress, expressly prohibit identifying a lawyer with the client's cause (Principle 18) and require freedom from prosecution for professional conduct (Principle 16). The prosecution of Lagovsky violates both principles; the refusal of all supervisory bodies to examine those violations is additional evidence of the systemic nature of the problem.

This is why all documents assembled here carry direct evidentiary value for the Serbian court examining the extradition request. They do not merely document violations — they document their systemic and irreversible character.
summary: Russia has stripped the applicant of access to any effective remedy. No court, no prosecutor, no General Prosecutor's Office examined a single substantive argument. Under the ECtHR approach in Othman, Mamatkulov, Golder and Kudła, that pattern is directly relevant to the extradition analysis and supports refusal where the requesting State offers no real judicial protection.
